title: Surjective images of semisimple Lie algebras in characteristic zero
statement: Let $F$ be a field of characteristic zero [def-weil-field], let $L,H$ be finite-dimensional $F$-Lie algebras [def-wf-lie-algebra], and let $q:L\to H$ be a surjective linear map satisfying $q([x,y])=[q(x),q(y)]$. If $L$ has no nonzero solvable Lie ideal, then $H$ has no nonzero solvable Lie ideal; thus semisimplicity in the sense of [def-wf-semisimple-lie-algebra] descends under surjective Lie homomorphisms.

source.place: §22c, printed p.475, final paragraph: for a representation with kernel ideal a, the Killing-form decomposition g=a⊕b has both summands semisimple. Apply the same ideal decomposition to ker(q).

proof.text: Put $I=\ker q$. It is an ideal: if $i\in I$ and $x\in L$, then $q([x,i])=[q(x),0]=0$. Apply [lem-sfb-semisimple-lie-ideal-complement] to $L$ and $I$, obtaining an ideal $J$ with $I\cap J=0$ and $I+J=L$. The field has characteristic zero, $L$ is finite-dimensional, and the hypothesis on its solvable ideals is exactly the semisimplicity required there.

source.place: §22c, printed p.475 (PDF p.487), final paragraph under The Casimir operator: the kernel ideal has a complementary ideal, obtained using the Killing form; characteristic-zero and finite-dimensional hypotheses at the start of §22c.

proof.text: The restriction $q_J:J\to H$ is injective since its kernel is $I\cap J=0$. It is surjective: for $h=q(x)$, write $x=i+j$ with $i\in I,j\in J$; then $h=q(j)$. Also $[I,J]=0$: a bracket $[i,j]$ lies in $J$ because $J$ is an ideal and in $I$ because $I$ is an ideal and the bracket is skew-symmetric, hence lies in $I\cap J$.

source.place: §22c, printed p.475 (PDF p.487), final paragraph under The Casimir operator: the kernel ideal has a complementary ideal, obtained using the Killing form; characteristic-zero and finite-dimensional hypotheses at the start of §22c.

proof.text: Let $A\subseteq H$ be a solvable ideal and put $B=\{j\in J:q(j)\in A\}$. This is a subspace and is an ideal of $L$: for $x=i+j\in I+J$ and $b\in B$, one has $[x,b]=[j,b]\in J$ and $q([j,b])=[q(j),q(b)]\in A$. Thus $[x,b]\in B$.

source.place: §22c, printed p.475 (PDF p.487), final paragraph under The Casimir operator: the kernel ideal has a complementary ideal, obtained using the Killing form; characteristic-zero and finite-dimensional hypotheses at the start of §22c.

proof.text: Choose $n$ with $D^nA=0$. Inductively $q(D^rB)\subseteq D^rA$: at $r=0$ this is the definition of $B$; the successor follows by mapping each bracket generator, using $q([u,v])=[q(u),q(v)]$ and linearity on their span. Hence $q(D^nB)=0$. Since $D^nB\subseteq B\subseteq J$ and $q_J$ is injective, $D^nB=0$. Thus $B$ is a solvable ideal of $L$, so $B=0$ by hypothesis. For $a\in A$, surjectivity of $q_J$ gives $j\in J$ with $q(j)=a$; this $j$ belongs to $B=0$, giving $a=0$. Every solvable ideal of $H$ is zero, which is its semisimplicity.
